title: John close: all the books in the world (John 21:20–25)
hook: if everything were written down, the world couldn't contain the books
carry: the world could not contain it

segments.voice: Yesterday, three questions by a charcoal fire. Your line was feed my sheep. Who did you look after? Day six hundred fifty-six, and the last day in John.

Peter has just been forgiven, given a job, and told follow me. And what's the very first thing he does? He turns around, sees the beloved disciple walking behind them, and asks: "Lord, and what shall this man do?" What about him? It's a very human question: barely handed a calling of his own, Peter is already checking someone else's. Is his harder? Easier? Does he get the better ending? Jesus's answer is short, and it's the last thing he says in John's Gospel.

"If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me." What is that to you? Your path is yours. And then John clears up a rumor. People had started saying this disciple would never die. John says, Jesus never said that. He only said, if I want him to stay, what is that to you? It seems the community needed that set straight, perhaps after the beloved disciple had died. Then a signature, of sorts: "This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true." We. Other voices, standing behind the witness, vouching for him. And then the last verse of the Gospel, with a wink: "there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written." A Gospel that began with the Word, before time, ends with books, more books than the world could hold. The Greek word is biblia, little scrolls, the word that gave us Bible. We've spent sixty-five days in this Gospel. Here's what we carried. The Word and the Lamb. Come and see, under the fig tree, water into wine. Born from above, for God so loved. A Samaritan woman at a well. Bread of life, light of the world, the truth will set you free. The good shepherd, Lazarus, Jesus wept. A grain of wheat, feet washed, a new commandment, many rooms, the vine. Then the garden, the fire, ecce homo, it is finished. And Rabboni, peace be with you, my Lord and my God, come and dine, feed my sheep. Tomorrow we open a letter, written by Paul, from prison, full of joy.
screen: `WHAT IS THAT TO THEE? FOLLOW THOU ME.`
`BIBLIA: MORE BOOKS THAN THE WORLD COULD HOLD.`
then, large: `THE WORLD ITSELF COULD NOT CONTAIN THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line of your own witness. Settle, and breathe. Think back over these weeks in John. Which scene stayed with you? A word, a line, a face. Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one that actually stuck. Now shape one sentence about it, in your own words. Something you've seen, or wondered, or felt. If you pray, it can be a line of thanks. If you're learning, it can be a question. After the sit, write it down somewhere you'll find it again. The bell holds the time.
John close. The end of the fourth Gospel: follow thou me, a witness vouched for, and more books than the world could hold.
Your line: the world could not contain it. Today, write your one line of witness down, and if someone asks what you're reading, tell them. Day six hundred fifty-six, and John is complete.

howItsDone: In many churches, readings from John fill the weeks of Lent and Easter, and some Christians read the Gospel straight through as a whole.

original.note: Greek: books, little scrolls. the last word of John's Gospel in Greek, and where 'Bible' comes from.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gospel ends by saying Jesus did a lot.
what it means: follow your own path, trust the witness, and know the story is bigger than any book.
what a scholar hears: a rumor corrected (21:23), a 'we' vouching for the beloved disciple (21:24), and biblia, the plural of biblion, a little scroll.
